judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: Scroll-down arrow at the bottom of the hero: <a onclick="scrollInto('sectionSocialMedia')"> with no href, holding a display:table div and an fa-angle-down icon. It is visible in the screenshot (circle with a chevron) with a pointer cursor, so users perceive it as a control. The claim says the browser-computed name is the U+F107 glyph, but the snapshot's CDP node shows role link, name "" (nameFrom contents) and Rampa's own browserName is empty, so the sentence is not true of the capture (claimTrue no). The element still fails 4.1.2: a scripted control that Chrome exposes as a link with no name (its role is also only generic by HTML-AAM, and it is not keyboard focusable, a 2.1.1 issue). Skeptic reasons checked: it is not hidden, not decorative, and the live page has the same markup (captureDiffers no); being a redundant convenience does not exempt it. The claim's point and fix (it has no usable text name; give it one) name the real failure in imperfect words: true_positive.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: News-card link whose content (h3 headline and summary, plus a photo in the image cards) sits inside an <article> element inside the <a>. The CDP tree in the snapshot shows Chrome exposing it as role link with name "" and no nameFrom: Chrome does not take name from content through the article role. The live page has the same markup, so captureDiffers is no, and claimTrue is yes for the captured browser name. Skeptic reasons that hold up: the link has visible text content (H91/G91 in markup), the accname recursion step and axe-core compute the full headline as its name, and screen readers in browse mode read the link's descendants, so 'announces only link' is not established. On the other hand the platform name Chrome exposes is empty, which matters for link lists, voice control and focus announcements. Whether that fails 4.1.2 depends on how assistive technologies handle the empty name, which the evidence does not show, and competent auditors would split, so elementFails is cannot_tell and the label is uncertain. Link: HU/UEL é aprovado em todos os critérios...

Skeptic checks: the text is real information (the data source), not incidental. Where the faint sketch shows through, the background is darker and the contrast lower still, so 3.34:1 is the best case, and the glyph stems reach the CSS colour #888. The live page serves the same CSS. true_positive.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: UEL FM 107,9 logo with alt="" in the radio block. Right above it is the radio player iframe, whose title is 'UEL FM radio player' (in the snapshot), and the player page itself (radio.uel.br/player, fetched now) shows the text 'Você está ouvindo Rádio UEL FM 107,9' and its own logo with alt 'Logo da UEL FM'. So the station name and frequency are in the text around the logo, the logo is redundant, and a null alt is the correct treatment (H67). The claim that the surrounding text does not say it is false: the frame's title says UEL FM (claimTrue no). The snapshot did not collect the cross-origin frame's content, which differs from what users receive and touches this claim (captureDiffers yes). Rampa lacked the frame's text: false_positive, context_missing.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: 'MAIS NOTÍCIAS' button-styled link below the secondary news cards, to https://operobal.uel.br/ (the university news portal, new tab). 'More news', placed after the news section (h2 'NOTÍCIAS', news h3 headlines before it), tells users the purpose: go to more news. Understanding 2.4.4 does not require naming the destination site. It is the only link with this name, so R1 does not apply. The live page is the same. The claim that the text does not tell where it goes is wrong: false_positive, model_error.
